questions.knowledge_point: Constructing a Vector Field From Its Stream Function
questions.problem: Construct the vector field that has the stream function $ψ(x,y)={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+x.$
questions.worked_solution:
A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if the following equations hold:

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}
$$

Computing the partial derivatives of the function $ψ(x,y),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{∂ψ}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+x) \\  & =2y, \\ Q & =-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x} \\  & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+x) \\  & =2x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field with the stream function $ψ(x,y)={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y) & =P\,i+Q\,j \\  & =2y\,i+(2x-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Cases Where a Stream Function Exists
questions.problem:
Which of the following vector fields have a stream function?

- $F(x,y)=y\,i-x\,j$
- $F(x,y)=xy\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$
- $F(x,y)=2x\,i-y\,j$
questions.worked_solution:
A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field I has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0+0=0
$$

- Vector field II doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=y+2y\ne 0.
$$

- Vector field III doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2+(-1)\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=y{e}^{x},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =x{e}^{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2xy+(-2)\ne 0.

questions.problem:
Which of the following is a stream function for the vector field
$F(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,i-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\,j?$
questions.worked_solution:
A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,i-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)$ and $Q(x,y)=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy).$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy),\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a no stream function, since 

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=(1-{x}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\ne 0.
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following is a stream function for the vector field
$F(x,y)=3({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,i-6xy\,j?$
questions.worked_solution:
A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)=3({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,i-6xy\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)=3({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})$ and $Q(x,y)=-6xy.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=6x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-6x.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=6x+(-6x)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}=3({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}),\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=6xy.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)=3{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)=3{x}^{2}y+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=0,$ and $g(y)=-{y}^{3},$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)=3{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}=2x,\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=2y.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)=2xy+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)=2xy+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)=2xy.
$$

Finally, we find the level curves of the stream function $ψ(x,y)=2xy$ given by the equations $ψ(x,y)=c.$

Notice that the range of $ψ(x,y)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ So, we will consider level curves for any value of $c.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =c \\ 2xy & =c \\ y & =\frac{c}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above gives us a family of hyperbolas with asymptotes $y=0$ and $x=0$ and, for $c=0,$ the lines $y=0$ and $x=0.$ Therefore, the correct graph (along with the vector field $F$) is as follows:

questions.problem: Determine the equation of the streamline that passes through the point $P(-1,-1)$ for the vector field $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i-2xy\,j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $F$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.
. 

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i-2xy\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=-2xy.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2x+(-2x)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}={x}^{2},\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=2xy.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y.
$$

Finally, we find the level curve of the stream function $ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y$ that passes through $P.$
First, we find the value of the stream function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(-1,-1) & =(-1)^{2}\cdot (-1) \\  & =1\cdot (-1) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the streamline that passes through $P(-1,-1)$ is the $-1$-level curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =-1 \\ {x}^{2}y & =-1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the streamline that passes through $P(-1,-1)$ is $y=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.$

questions.problem: Determine the equation of the streamline that passes through the point $P(0,\pi )$ for the vector field $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,i-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $F$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.
. 

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,i-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+(-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.
$$

Finally, we find the level curve of the stream function $ψ(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ that passes through $P.$
First, we find the value of the stream function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(0,\pi ) & ={e}^{(0)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the streamline that passes through $P(0,\pi )$ is the $0$-level curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our possible streamlines are $y=k\pi $ for any integer $k.$ The streamline that passes through $P(0,\pi )$ is $y=\pi .$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Constructing a Vector Field From Its Stream Function
canonical_examples.problem: Construct the vector field that has the stream function $\psi(x,y) = e^{x} \cos{y}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A function $\psi(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf F= P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ if the following equations hold:

$$
P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y},\qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}
$$

Computing the partial derivatives of the function $\psi(x,y),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{∂ψ}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y, \\ Q & =-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x} \\  & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field with the stream function $\psi(x,y) = e^{x} \cos{y}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y) & =P\,i+Q\,j \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,i-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining Cases Where a Stream Function Exists
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following vector fields have a stream function?

- $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = x^4y\,\mathbf{i} - 2x^3y^2\,\mathbf{j}$

- $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \sin x \sin y\,\mathbf{i} + \cos x \cos y\,\mathbf{j}$

- $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = 4x^2y\,\mathbf{i} -4x^2y^2\,\mathbf{j}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A vector field $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ with a simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ has a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field I has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4{x}^{3}y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-4{x}^{3}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
= 4x^3y + (- 4x^3y)
= 0
$$

- Vector field II has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
= \cos x \sin y + (- \cos x \sin y)
= 0.
$$

- Vector field III doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=8xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-8{x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
= 8xy + (- 8x^2y)
\neq 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining a Stream Function for a Vector Field
canonical_examples.problem:
Find a stream function for the vector field $\mathbf F,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y) = 2y\,\mathbf{i} +2x\,\mathbf{j}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A vector field $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ with a simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ has a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.
$$

Note that $\mathbf{F}(x,y) =  2y\,\mathbf{i} +2x\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D=\mathbb{R}^2,$ where $P(x,y) = 2y$ and $Q(x,y) =2x.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\mathbf F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0 + 0 = 0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $\psi(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf F= P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ if 

$$
P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} = 2y, \qquad \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} = -2x.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
\psi(x,y) = y^2 + f(x), \qquad 
\psi(x,y) = -x^2+ g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f(x)=-x^2$ and $g(y)=y^2,$ we have

$$
\psi(x,y) = y^2-x^2.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Determine the equation of the streamline that passes through the point $P(-1,1)$ for the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (x^3-3xy^2)\,\mathbf{i} + (y^3-3x^2y)\,\mathbf{j}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.

A vector field $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ with a simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ has a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.
$$

Note that $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (x^3-3xy^2)\,\mathbf{i} + (y^3-3x^2y)\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D=\mathbb{R}^2,$ where $P(x,y) = x^3-3xy^2$ and $Q(x,y) = y^3 - 3x^2y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =3{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\mathbf F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = (3x^2-3y^2) + (3y^2 - 3x^2) = 0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $\psi(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf F= P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ if 

$$
P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} = x^3-3xy^2, \qquad \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} = -y^3+3x^2y.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
\psi(x,y) = x^3y - xy^3 + f(x), \qquad 
\psi(x,y) = -xy^3 + x^3y + g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
\psi(x,y) = x^3y - xy^3.
$$

Finally, we find the level curve of the stream function $\psi(x,y) = x^3y - xy^3$ that passes through $P.$
First, we find the value of the stream function at $P{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(-1,1) & =(-1)^{3}(1)-(-1)(1)^{3} \\  & =-1-(-1) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the streamline that passes through $P(-1,1)$ is the $0$-level curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =0 \\ {x}^{3}y-x{y}^{3} & =0 \\ xy({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ xy(x+y)(x-y) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our possible streamlines are $x=0,$ $y=0,$ $y=-x,$ or $y=x.$ The streamline that passes through $P(-1,1)$ is $y=-x.$
The vector field and the streamline through the point $P$ are shown below.
